description: Compare all three qualitative current-voltage panels within the explicitly stated reverse non-breakdown range, without reading numerical currents or voltages from the sketches.

authoritativeText.text: 111. Current across the junction between p-type and n-type semiconductors

In Figure 224, the left half of the sample contains donor impurities and is an $n$-type semiconductor.
Free electrons are the more numerous charge carriers there.

The right half contains acceptor impurities and is a $p$-type semiconductor, where holes are the more numerous charge carriers.
A hole is a vacancy left by an electron, and its movement can also produce current.

When the two semiconductor types are adjacent, their boundary is called a $p-n$ junction.
These letters identify the conduction types.

They do not mean that the two whole regions carry negative and positive net charges, respectively.
After the regions are joined, electrons and holes diffuse from the side where each is more numerous toward the side where it is less numerous.

Near the boundary, electrons fill holes, leaving charged impurity ions that cannot move freely.
These ions produce a built-in electric field.

The field opposes further diffusion of majority carriers and creates a built-in potential barrier, an energy threshold for crossing the boundary.
Without an external power supply, once equilibrium is reached, diffusion and the opposing motion caused by the field balance.
There is no sustained net current.

Connect the sample as in Figure 225: the battery's positive terminal to the $p$-type side and its negative terminal to the $n$-type side.
The first side is at a positive potential and the second at a negative potential, so the first side has the higher potential.

The applied voltage reduces the barrier that previously opposed diffusion.
The region near the boundary with few free charge carriers also becomes narrower.

Current through the $p-n$ junction is now mainly produced by majority carriers crossing the boundary.
Electrons diffuse from the $n$ region to the $p$ region, and holes diffuse from the $p$ region to the $n$ region.
The battery continually supplies charge, allowing the process to continue rather than occurring only at the instant of connection.

Electrons move opposite to the conventional current direction.
Holes move in the same direction as conventional current.
With this connection, the sample conducts readily and has a relatively small resistance.

This connection is called forward bias, and the current is called forward current.
Figure 226a shows the forward current-voltage characteristic: the relationship between current and applied voltage.

This lesson considers only reverse voltages too small to cause breakdown.
A sufficiently large reverse voltage can produce a large reverse current.
This is called reverse breakdown and is outside this lesson's scope.

Reverse the battery connections: connect the side previously attached to the positive terminal to the negative terminal, and vice versa.
For the same voltage magnitude, the circuit current is much smaller than with forward bias.

The applied voltage now increases the built-in barrier, and the region near the boundary with few free carriers becomes wider.
It is harder for majority carriers to cross the boundary.

A small current can still flow, mainly because of the other type of carrier, which is less numerous.
Electrons cross from the $p$ region to the $n$ region, and holes cross from the $n$ region to the $p$ region.
Free electrons are less numerous in a $p$-type semiconductor.

Holes are less numerous in an $n$-type semiconductor.
These less numerous carriers are called minority carriers.

The number of majority carriers therefore cannot be used to estimate the current crossing the boundary here.
Within the operating range considered in this lesson, the sample conducts poorly and has a very large reverse resistance.
The current is small, but it is not entirely absent.

This small current is called reverse current;
its current-voltage characteristic appears in Figure 226b.

Figure 226c combines the forward and reverse current-voltage characteristics of the $p-n$ junction.
Figures 226a, b, and c explain the processes at the boundary between $p$-type and $n$-type semiconductors only qualitatively.
They show trends, not exact current or voltage values that can be read from the diagrams.

The actual forward and reverse currents differ greatly.
Do not treat these schematic diagrams as measurements showing currents of similar magnitude.

**A $p-n$ junction behaves differently for the two directions of current.
The forward resistance of a $p-n$ junction is much smaller than its reverse resistance.**

This asymmetry of the $p-n$ junction can be used to rectify alternating current.
Alternating current repeatedly changes direction.

The junction readily allows forward current but greatly reduces reverse current, producing current that mainly flows in one direction.
The rectified current may still vary with time.
A mostly consistent direction does not by itself mean a constant current magnitude.

inventory.description: Left panel has an upward vertical axis, rightward horizontal axis starting at their intersection, an I-form current glyph, a V-form voltage glyph, an unresolved oval glyph near the origin and an a-shaped source subpart glyph below. One finite solid curve starts at the origin and rises to the right with increasing steepness, ending below/right of the vertical arrow tip. No negative-axis extension in this panel and no curve continuation arrow.

Middle panel has an upward vertical axis, a horizontal axis extending left of the origin and pointing right, I-form above, minus-V-form below the left extension, V-form below the right arrow, an unresolved oval near the origin and a be-shaped subpart mark below. One finite solid curve starts below the left horizontal extension and rises shallowly toward the origin. There is no positive-side curve or breakdown turn.

Right panel has an upward vertical axis, left horizontal extension and right-pointing arrow, I-form above, minus-V-form left, V-form right, unresolved oval near the origin and a ve-shaped subpart mark below. A finite shallow negative-side solid branch below the left extension meets the origin and continues as a finite steeply rising positive-side solid branch. The common origin and two joined branches share one frame. No breakdown branch, grid, tick or data dot.

All three panels appear horizontally together; their differing axis heights and finite endpoint positions are visible. Six axis arrowheads, four finite branches (two joined in the right panel), three oval origin glyphs, three subpart glyphs, three I-form labels, three right V-form labels and two separate left minus-V-form labels. No numbered scales, ticks, grid, measured current/voltage values or curve arrows.
